content: The references provided are a collection of studies and articles related to the use, complications, and management of peripheral intravenous (IV) catheters and central venous catheters (CVCs) in various patient populations, including neonates, children, and adults. 1. Oliveira and Parreira (2012) investigated the incidence of phlebitis in patients with peripheral intravenous catheters and analyzed the influence of specific risk factors. Their findings highlight the importance of identifying and mitigating these risks to improve patient outcomes. 2. Tsai et al. (2009) compared complication rates associated with central venous catheters inserted at femoral versus non-femoral sites in very low birth weight infants. Their study provides critical insights into site selection for catheter placement in this vulnerable population. 3. Wrightson (2013) examined complications of peripherally inserted central catheters (PICCs) in neonates, comparing upper versus lower extremity insertion sites. The study emphasizes the need for careful site selection to minimize adverse events. 4. Tseng et al. (2023) explored factors affecting the patency and complications of peripheral intravenous catheters in newborns. Their findings underscore the importance of catheter care and maintenance in neonatal populations. 5. Lee et al. (2009) conducted a prospective study involving 3,165 hospitalized patients to identify risk factors for peripheral intravenous catheter infections. Their research provides valuable data for infection prevention strategies. 6. Almonte et al. (1999) compared two methods of securing peripheral intravenous cannulas, focusing on their effectiveness and safety. The study offers practical recommendations for clinical practice. 7. Callaghan et al. (2002) evaluated two methods of securing peripheral intravenous cannulas in pediatric settings, providing evidence-based guidance for improving catheter stability and reducing complications. 8. Chico-Padron et al. (2011) assessed the safety and cost-effectiveness of transparent versus gauze wound dressings for intravenous catheterization. Their findings support the use of transparent dressings for better outcomes. 9. Craven et al. (1985) conducted a randomized study comparing transparent polyurethane dressings to dry gauze dressings for peripheral intravenous catheter sites. The study highlights the benefits of transparent dressings in reducing bacterial colonization. 10. Downing and Charles (1987) compared the use of transparent polyurethane dressings with conventional techniques for intravenous cannula fixation and dressing. Their research provides insights into the advantages of modern dressing materials. 11. Hoffmann et al. (1988) investigated the risk of bacterial colonization and phlebitis associated with transparent polyurethane film dressings for peripheral intravenous sites. Their findings emphasize the need for careful dressing selection. 12. Kelsey and Gosling (1984) compared morbidity associated with occlusive and non-occlusive dressings applied to peripheral intravenous devices. The study provides evidence for the selection of appropriate dressing types. 13. Littenberg and Thompson (1987) tested a new technology comparing gauze versus plastic for peripheral intravenous dressings. Their research highlights the potential benefits of advanced dressing materials. 14. Machado et al. (2008) examined adverse events related to the use of peripheral intravenous catheters in children, focusing on the impact of different dressing regimens. Their findings inform best practices for pediatric catheter care. 15. Madeo et al. (1997) conducted a randomized study comparing IV3000 transparent polyurethane dressings to dry gauze dressings for peripheral intravenous catheter sites. The study supports the use of transparent dressings for improved outcomes. 16. Maki and Ringer (1987) evaluated dressing regimens for preventing infections with peripheral intravenous catheters, comparing gauze, transparent polyurethane dressings, and iodophor-transparent dressings. Their findings guide infection prevention strategies. 17. Meylan (1987) assessed the increased risk of bacterial colonization of intravenous catheters covered with transparent adhesive polyurethane bandages compared to classical gauze bandages. The study highlights the need for careful dressing selection. 18. Peterson and Freeman (1982) explored the use of transparent polyurethane dressings for peripheral intravenous catheter care, providing evidence for their effectiveness in clinical practice. 19. Popovsky and Ilstrup (1986) examined the impact of dressing types on peripheral intravenous catheter sites, contributing to the understanding of optimal dressing practices. 20. San Martin Rodriguez et al. (2002) compared transparent dressings with gauze for venous blood vessel maintenance, providing evidence for the benefits of transparent dressings in clinical settings. 21. Tripepi-Bova et al. (1997) analyzed rates of phlebitis, infiltration, and dislodgment at catheter sites, offering insights into patient outcomes and catheter management. 22. Vanden Bosch et al. (1997) evaluated the use of adhesive bandage dressing regimens for peripheral venous catheters, contributing to evidence-based practice in catheter care. 23. Arredondo et al. (2021) assessed the safety and efficacy of developmental wing guides and hybrid guides for wire-in-needle PICC cannulation, providing recommendations for neonatal care. 24. Salles et al. (2007) conducted a cost-effectiveness analysis of peripheral catheter dressings, offering insights into resource allocation and patient care. 25. Ni Chronin et al. (2022) studied the burden of peripheral intravenous catheters in older hospitalized patients, contributing to the understanding of catheter-related complications in geriatric populations. 26. Da Silva et al. (2010) highlighted the benefits of establishing an intravenous team and standardizing peripheral intravenous catheter care, emphasizing the importance of specialized teams in improving outcomes. 27. Levit et al. (2020) examined the impact of a dedicated nursing team on central line-related complications in neonatal intensive care units, providing evidence for team-based approaches to catheter care. 28. Meier et al. (1998) evaluated the impact of a dedicated intravenous therapy team on nosocomial bloodstream infection rates, supporting the role of specialized teams in infection prevention. 29. Pitts (2013) conducted a retrospective analysis of a pediatric vascular access program, providing insights into clinical outcomes and program effectiveness. 30. Scally et al. (1992) studied the impact of an intravenous therapy team on the occurrence of intravenous-related phlebitis, offering evidence for team-based interventions. 31. Soifer et al. (1998) conducted a randomized controlled trial to prevent peripheral venous catheter complications with an intravenous therapy team, providing evidence for improved patient outcomes. 32. Tomford et al. (1984) evaluated the role of an intravenous therapy team in reducing peripheral venous catheter-associated complications, supporting the implementation of specialized teams. 33. Trent (1984) investigated peripheral-associated phlebitis, contributing to the understanding of risk factors and prevention strategies. 34. Yongshu et al. (2019) evaluated the role of a PICC team in preventing mechanical phlebitis in very-low-birth-weight premature infants, providing evidence for team-based care in neonates. 35. Martínez et al. (2020) discussed an approach to antibiotic treatment in patients with sepsis, offering guidance for clinical management. 36. Fujioka et al. (2020) compared pain perception during short peripheral catheter placement by a structured vascular access team versus bedside nurses, emphasizing the benefits of specialized teams. 37. Ballantyne et al. (2003) evaluated the efficacy of tetracaine gel for pain relief during PICC placement in infants, providing evidence for pain management strategies. 38. Fein et al. (1998) studied the use of saline with benzyl alcohol as intradermal anesthesia for intravenous line placement in children, offering insights into pain reduction techniques. 39. Lemyre et al. (2006) assessed the effectiveness of tetracaine 4% gel in reducing procedural pain during PICC placement in infants, contributing to evidence-based pain management. 40. Schreiber et al. (2013) investigated whether EMLA cream application interferes with venipuncture or venous cannulation success, providing evidence for its use in clinical practice. 41. Taddio et al. (2005) evaluated liposomal lidocaine for improving procedural success rates and reducing pain in children, supporting its use in pediatric care. 42. Teillol-Foo and Kassab (1991) conducted a randomized controlled trial on topical glyceryl trinitrate and eutectic mixtures of local anesthetics in children, providing evidence for their effectiveness. 43. Zempsky et al. (2008) studied a needle-free powder lidocaine delivery system for venipuncture or cannulation pain in children, offering a novel approach to pain management. 44. Zhang et al. (2014) examined whether wearing gloves during pediatric peripheral intravenous cannulation adversely affects clinical performance, providing evidence for infection control practices. 45. Papa and Zempsky (2010) surveyed nurse perceptions of the impact of pediatric peripheral venous access pain on nurse and patient satisfaction, highlighting the importance of pain management. 46. Webb (1987) compared intravenous therapy methods in preterm infants, focusing on scalp vein needles versus Teflon catheters, providing evidence for optimal device selection. 47. Hoff et al. (2019) compared continuous infusion versus intermittent flushing of peripheral cannulas in neonates using needleless connectors, offering insights into catheter maintenance. 48. Kalyn et al. (2000) compared continuous infusion and intermittent flushing methods in peripheral intravenous catheters in neonates, contributing to evidence-based practice. 49. Perez et al. (2012) demonstrated that intermittent flushing improves cannula patency compared to continuous infusion for peripheral venous catheters in newborns, providing practical recommendations. 50. Stok and Wieringa (2016) compared continuous infusion versus intermittent flushing for maintaining peripheral intravenous access in newborn infants, offering evidence for clinical decision-making. 51. Tseng et al. (2022) explored factors affecting the patency and complications of peripheral intravenous catheters in newborns, emphasizing the importance of catheter care. 52. Witkowski et al. (2013) found no difference between continuous versus intermittent heparin infusion in maintaining intra-arterial catheter patency in postoperative pediatric surgery, providing evidence for practice. 53. Yeung et al. (2020) compared saline-lock versus continuous infusion for maintaining peripheral intravenous catheter access in children, offering evidence for resource optimization. 54. Araujo et al. (2011) concluded that intermittent heparin is not effective at preventing occlusion of peripherally inserted central venous catheters in preterm and term neonates, providing evidence for alternative approaches. 55. Arnts et al. (2011) compared heparin solution versus normal saline in maintaining patency of intravenous locks in neonates, offering evidence for clinical practice. 56. Bertolino et al. (2012) compared intermittent flushing with heparin versus saline for maintaining peripheral intravenous catheters in a medical department, providing evidence for cost-effective care. 57. Bowers et al. (2008) compared occlusion rates by flushing solutions for peripherally inserted central catheters with positive pressure Luer-activated devices, offering insights into catheter maintenance. 58. Brown et al. (1999) concluded that heparin is not required for peripheral intravenous locks in neonates, providing evidence for saline use. 59. Cook et al. (2011) compared heparinized saline versus normal saline for maintaining intravenous access in neonates, offering evidence for practice change. 60. Fujita et al. (2006) evaluated normal saline flushing for maintaining peripheral intravenous sites, providing evidence for its effectiveness. 61. Geritz (1992) compared saline versus heparin in intermittent infuser patency maintenance, offering evidence for clinical decision-making. 62. Gyr et al. (1995) conducted a double-blind comparison of heparin and saline flush solutions in maintaining peripheral infusion devices, providing evidence for practice. 63. Hanrahan et al. (2000) evaluated a change in practice to saline for peripheral intravenous locks in neonates, providing evidence for its effectiveness. 64. Heilskov et al. (1998) conducted a randomized trial of heparin and saline for maintaining intravenous locks in neonates, offering evidence for clinical practice. 65. Jonker et al. (2010) compared heparin versus saline during a period of heparin shortage, providing evidence for alternative solutions. 66. Kleiber et al. (1998) compared heparin versus saline locks in children, providing evidence for clinical decision-making.
